question.knowledge_point: Integrating a Logarithmic Expression Using Cyclic Integration by Parts
question.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int \frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={ln}^{9}⁡x & \,⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{9{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4x} & \,⇒\,v=\int \frac{1}{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int \frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({ln}^{9}⁡x)(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4})(\frac{9{ln}^{8}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{4}-9\int \frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{4}-9I.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $I.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{4}-9I \\ 10I & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{4} \\ I & =\frac{{ln}^{10}⁡x}{40}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{{ln}^{9}⁡x}{4x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{40}({ln}^{10}⁡x){|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{1}{40}({ln}^{10}⁡(e)-{ln}^{10}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{40}\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Indefinite Integral of a Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts
question.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(2{e}^{2x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{2x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(2{e}^{2x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2J \\ I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2(-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2I) \\ I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-4I \\ 5I & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{2x}}{5}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Indefinite Integral of a Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts
question.worked_solution:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{6x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6{e}^{6x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(6{e}^{6x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{6x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6{e}^{6x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(6{e}^{6x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6\int {e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6I.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6J \\ I & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6({e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-6I) \\ I & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6{e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-36I \\ 37I & =-{e}^{6x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+6{e}^{6x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{6x}}{37}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Definite Integral of a Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts
question.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{3x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(3{e}^{3x})\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{3x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{3x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{3x}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(3{e}^{3x})\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3\int {e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3I.\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I:$

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3J \\ I & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3(-{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3I) \\ I & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-9I \\ 10I & ={e}^{3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ I & =\frac{{e}^{3x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{e}^{3x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =(\frac{{e}^{3x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{10}){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2\pi )}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi ))}{10}-\frac{{e}^{3(0)}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))}{10} \\  & =\frac{3{e}^{6\pi }}{10}-\frac{3}{10} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}({e}^{6\pi }-1)\end{aligned}
$$
